items.stem: A Massachusetts Category 2 sterile compounding pharmacy uses a commercially manufactured SINGLE-DOSE vial as a component for future CSPs. At 8:00 a.m. a qualified compounder first punctures its intact septum inside a certified ISO Class 5 PEC. The vial is then stored OUTSIDE the ISO Class 5 PEC, at the manufacturer's specified refrigerated temperature; the closure remains intact and all other component requirements are satisfied. At 4:00 p.m. the same day the pharmacy plans another compounding use. Which conclusions are supported by USP's official <797> FAQ? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: Initial puncture in ISO Class 5 with suitable storage can support using the vial for up to 12 hours after first entry, assuming no shorter stability or other restriction applies.
choices.why: Correct. FAQ Q186 establishes the initial-entry condition and up-to-12-hour component-use period, subject to maintained storage conditions.

choices.text: Once the vial leaves the PEC after puncture, it must be discarded immediately because all post-entry storage is required to remain in ISO Class 5 air.
choices.why: Incorrect. FAQ Q186 says opened or punctured conventional single-dose containers may be stored outside the PEC under conditions.

choices.text: The pharmacy's 4:00 p.m. use may remain within the in-use period; the container must still be properly handled in the PEC when entered for compounding.
choices.why: Correct. Eight hours have passed since first entry, less than the conditional 12-hour maximum.

choices.text: An opened single-dose glass ampule may be saved for twelve hours by refrigerating the open neck, because ampules follow the same resealable-vial rule.
choices.why: Incorrect. FAQ Q186 distinguishes opened ampules: they cannot be stored after opening.

items.notes: USP official FAQ directly reviewed, but full subscription normative §15.1 original remains a legal source check before final approval.

items.stem: A Massachusetts sterile-compounding pharmacy prepares hazardous drugs in a suitable containment PEC. The staff propose a cleaning procedure that applies 70% isopropyl alcohol as the ONLY step because it disinfects work surfaces. Which statements reflect the distinct hazardous-drug controls described by USP <800> and OSHA's guidance? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: Using alcohol to disinfect alone is proven to deactivate all currently listed hazardous drugs.
choices.why: Incorrect. OSHA notes that alcohol-based disinfection does not automatically deactivate hazardous residues and may spread contamination.

choices.text: A visibly clean work surface may skip hazardous-drug decontamination because microbial disinfection is the only contamination concern.
choices.why: Incorrect. Visible appearance does not prove absence of hazardous drug residue or eliminate exposure controls.

choices.text: Deactivation, decontamination, and cleaning address hazardous-drug residues and soil, while subsequent disinfection in sterile compounding addresses microbial contamination.
choices.why: Correct. The distinct processes cannot be assumed equivalent; OSHA describes deactivation/decontamination/cleaning followed by disinfection for sterile work areas.

choices.text: The facility should assess its drug, materials and manufacturer instructions to choose appropriate residue-control steps rather than relying on one disinfectant alone.
choices.why: Correct. No single method has been found to deactivate all hazardous drugs; controls must fit actual substances and equipment.

items.citation: USP <800> §15 and Table 5 (official USP 2019 revision bulletin; 2026 text version not authenticated); OSHA Hazardous Drugs: Controlling Occupational Exposure; USP January 2026 <800> FAQ status
items.notes: 2026-11-18 VERIFICATION ADVANCE: Directly inspected USP's own 2019 Revision Bulletin, chapter <800> §15 and Table 5 (distinct residue control vs disinfection) and OSHA's current workplace page; USP Jan 21 2026 FAQ acknowledges current <800> is in USP–NF/Compounding Compendium and FAQ itself is not official normative interpretation. Do NOT assume unchanged normative 2026 version. Item remains legal HOLD pending chapter-version consistency.

additional_sources.support: Alcohol disinfection is not deactivation; no universal deactivation process
Current official chapter in paid compendium; FAQ expressly not an official interpretation

items.stem: A corporate Massachusetts pharmacy has a current DEA registration and an employee with an otherwise valid power of attorney (POA) to execute paper DEA Form 222 orders. An administrative employee who signed the pharmacy's last DEA registration application, but is NOT a corporate officer, now wants to revoke that POA in November 2026. The corporate vice president is an authorized officer and two witnesses are available. What is required under the March 20, 2026 revision to 21 CFR 1305.05?

choices.text: Only the employee holding the POA may terminate the arrangement, and the registrant cannot act without that consent.
choices.why: Incorrect. 21 CFR 1305.05(b) permits a registrant to revoke the POA at any time.

choices.text: Revocation requires destruction of every historical DEA Form 222 the employee previously signed, because records are void when POA authority ends.
choices.why: Incorrect. Previously executed order records and powers of attorney have retention requirements; revocation is not deletion of history.

choices.text: The administrative application signer can revoke the POA alone because signing the most recent registration application is sufficient federal authority.
choices.why: Incorrect. That older signatory language was specifically removed from §1305.05(c),(e) in 2026.

choices.text: A corporate officer, not the last registration application signer, must execute revocation with two witnesses and written notice.
choices.why: Correct. The current §1305.05(e) requires the registrant/partner/officer, as appropriate, and two witnesses; the notice and record duties remain.

items.notes: VERY HIGH-YIELD VERSION TRAP: DEA online 2020 FAQ still describes revoked-by-last-registration-application-signer; March 2026 amended binding regulation instead requires registrant, partner or corporate officer.

items.stem: A Massachusetts pharmacy sends a refrigerated prescription medication by courier to a patient's home. The insulated shipping container looks undamaged at delivery, but the temperature logger shows that the medication was exposed to a temperature outside its labeled storage range for an extended period. The manufacturer has not yet supplied stability data for that excursion. The patient requests that the courier leave the medication immediately. What is the BEST next step?

choices.text: Release the product because a sealed undamaged outer carton proves the medication's chemical stability despite the logger result.
choices.why: Incorrect. A good-looking exterior is not evidence that the product remained within required storage conditions.

choices.text: Hold the shipment, assess product integrity against stability evidence, and document the excursion before dispensing.
choices.why: Correct. 247 CMR 9.02(2) requires shipping not to impair integrity and §9.22 requires an out-of-range response and medication-integrity assessment.

choices.text: Ignore the logger because the medication was only in the courier's possession, not in the pharmacy's refrigerator.
choices.why: Incorrect. The dispensing pharmacy remains responsible for packing, transportation and delivery processes that protect integrity.

choices.text: Reset the package temperature indicator and leave the medication as long as the patient's name is correct on the label.
choices.why: Incorrect. Replacing evidence or relabeling does not assess the quality of a temperature-exposed product.

items.citation: 247 CMR 9.02(2); 247 CMR 9.22(1),(4); Massachusetts Board pharmacy storage-shipping guidance
items.notes: The available fact is an unassessed excursion, not proof that drug must always be destroyed.
